newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Grain-Market still looks for bottom.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Grain-Market still looks for bottom.

text.p: Australian cash grains prices remained flat in low-level trading during the past week, with so little interest that a late kick in the sorghum price provided the highlight of the week.
Cash sorghum rose by about A$6.00 a tonne to about A$195 (Newcastle) or A$200 (Sydney), according to one trader, or by A$6.00 to A$204 August delivery Sydney, according to another.
"It's very quiet," said Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders.

Drifting cash prices, hesitant futures prices and a lack of trade on world markets saw the week close with the main unanswered question of whether the wheat market had hit bottom, signalling the prospect of an upturn.
"Most people seem to think it has a little more weakness, a little more to go," Cameron Pratt of GrainCorp said.
"I believe so," said Howard, asked if the market had bottomed.
"I think we're just trying to see where the low is at the moment," said Brendon Hillary of ANZ McCaughan Futures Ltd.
Sorghum's price kick was more the result of selling resistance by farmers at present prices than a sign of market life, traders told Reuters.
Cash wheat prices fell A$4-A$5 over the week, with a little new crop November/December delivery Newcastle trading at A$183.

The Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) indicative price for old crop Australian Standard White (ASW) wheat was steady at A$210 a tonne delivered Sydney on a Friday-to-Friday basis. New crop ASW delivered Newcastle edged back to A$182 from A$183, while all other quoted classes also fell by A$1 a tonne.
Feed barley fell by about A$5 over the week to A$145 for southern feedlots or to about A$160 for northern feedlots.
Howard said for the market to break out of the doldrums the Sydney Futures Exchange January would need to rise to A$220 from its present level of about A$190 for the January contract.
Farmer hedging would emerge at this level, he said.
"But until we see a A$20 or A$30 movement, I think they're just going to sit back and do nothing," he said.
Hillary said the futures market was unlikely to begin to move until the cash market moved.
"If you haven't got any forward sales you've got nothing... risk-wise and so no reason to do any business," he said.
But with the U.S. spring wheat harvest in satisfactory progress, there were no forces one way or the other, he said.
"We're just waiting to see that the low is in place and then you'll see a lot more confidence in decision-making," he said.
Australia scored no international wheat sales during the week. A 150,000 tonne purchase of U.S. wheat by Egypt still left U.S. exports well down, AWB spokesman Alex Nichol said.
"It really is very dull right around the world," he said, adding the market needed a big sale to break out.

A drifting Australian futures market left most interest to options trading. Friday's trade of four A$205 January call options at a A$6 premium, outnumbering the single January futures trade at A$190 a tonne, was typical of the week's tone.
Over the week, the most commonly traded contract, January 1997, fell to A$191.50 from A$193.50 on a Friday-to-Friday settlement basis.
